ACCEPT. The coefficient-one theorem, the zero-charge calculation for every straight-comb alignment, and the pure-rectangle extension follow from the supplied arguments. The mixed capped extension also follows using the explicitly permitted capped receiver result under its stated hypotheses.I found no counterexample or logical gap in these conclusions. The points that require particular care are the cancellation of saturated transfers within a complete receiver, the exterior guards in the rectangle reduction, and preservation of the capped receivers throughout normalization. Each can be justified directly, without enumeration.1. Tile ownership and the closed-receiver ledger are validThe ownership argument uses precisely the right graph: the graph induced by the actual matching endpoints.For a unit square, the only nonempty disconnected induced subset of its four-cycle is a pair of opposite corners. If these are  $P$ , each other corner has two  $P$ -neighbors and therefore cannot be  $T$ . With neither remaining corner in  $P$ , both are blank. Either  $P$ -corner consequently has at most two occupied neighbors, contradicting single-terminality.This proves ownership for aligned tiles and for unaligned unit squares. It also handles the physical boundary: extending by blanks can only reduce the number of occupied neighbors available.There is no hidden matching-closure assumption in the subsequent ledger. If  $x\in H$ , its actual matching mate is adjacent to  $x$  and belongs to  $P$ , so it belongs to the same endpoint component  $H$ . Thus the collection  $R_H$  is closed under actual matching mates.For clarity, define the raw excess of any tile by
$$e(Q)=t_Q+\frac{p_Q}{2}-2.$$
Then the supplied charge convention gives
$$\rho(Q)=
\begin{cases}
e(Q)+s_Q/2,&Q\text{ deficient},\\
0,&Q\text{ saturated}.
\end{cases}$$
The saturated-tile facts used here are also consistent with the feasibility condition:Three selected vertices in a four-cycle would give one selected vertex two selected neighbors, so  $t_Q\le2$ .If a saturated tile’s two selected vertices are adjacent, the other two vertices are blank.If they are opposite, at most one of the other two vertices can be occupied. Hence a saturated tile has at most one  $P$ , and no internal matching edge.A matching edge between two saturated tiles is impossible. At the shared tile boundary, the selected neighbors forced by saturation would give a selected vertex both its  $P$ -neighbor and an adjacent selected neighbor.Consequently, a saturated tile has
$$e(Q)=p_Q/2,$$
and its possible endpoint has its mate in a deficient tile.For a closed receiver, this yields the exact calculation
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho(R_H)
&=\sum_{Q\in R_H}e(Q)
 +\frac12\left(
 \sum_{\substack{Q\in R_H\\Q\text{ deficient}}}s_Q
 -
 \sum_{\substack{Q\in R_H\\Q\text{ saturated}}}p_Q
 \right)\\
&=\sum_{Q\in R_H}e(Q).
\end{aligned}$$
The parenthesized expression vanishes: each saturated endpoint in the receiver has exactly one actual mate in a deficient receiver tile, and every incidence counted by the first sum arises this way.Tile ownership now gives
$$\sum_{Q\in R_H}p_Q=|H|,$$
so
$$\rho(R_H)
=
|T\cap V(R_H)|+\frac{|H|}{2}-2|R_H|.$$
This establishes Main Note (2) with the original physical tile charges. In particular, the argument does not require an individual deficient tile to have nonpositive charge.Finally,  $R_H$  and  $Z$  partition the physical tiles. On every tile of  $Z$ , including a saturated one,
$$\rho(Q)=t_Q-2.$$
Therefore the decomposition
$$|T|+|M|-\frac{mn}{2}
=
\sum_H\rho(R_H)-\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q)$$
is exact. Each physical tile, each selected vertex counted through its tile, and each saturated matching transfer enters this calculation once.2. The structural dependency applies componentwiseThe supplied turn and branch proofs are sound.In the turn proof, the selected neighbor of the turning vertex forces one neighboring site blank. Terminality of the adjacent endpoint then forces the opposite corner of the proposed square occupied; that corner cannot be selected because it already has two endpoint neighbors. It is therefore  $P$ .In the branch proof, the two candidate square-completing sites cannot be selected. If both were blank, the intervening endpoint would have occupied degree at most two. Thus one is  $P$ .Every square produced by either argument belongs to the same endpoint component as the original vertex. Accordingly, these arguments have the componentwise consequence needed later:In a globally single-terminal configuration, an endpoint component containing no  $P$ -square is a straight even path, even if other components contain  $P$ -squares.The matching on that path is its unique perfect matching. Matching edges cannot leave the component, and a finite path has a perfect matching exactly when its order is even.The support argument also works for a straight complete component in an arbitrary feasible exterior. All perpendicular sites adjacent to the path, and the outward axial sites at its ends, are outside  $P$  by component completeness.If a path vertex had both perpendicular neighbors selected, either adjacent path vertex would have both perpendicular sites forced blank. That adjacent vertex would then have at most two occupied neighbors. This remains true when it is itself a path end: its two axial directions supply at most two occupied neighbors in total. Hence every path vertex has at most one perpendicular selected support.Terminality supplies the rest:An inner vertex has exactly one perpendicular  $T$ .An end has exactly one perpendicular  $T$  and its outward axial neighbor in  $T$ .Consecutive perpendicular supports must lie on opposite sides, since otherwise they would be adjacent selected vertices, each already incident to a  $P$ .Thus the alternating comb structure follows for every  $r\ge1$ , including the two-endpoint case.The stronger freezing statement in the supplied structural proof is also justified. Each path end has two permanent selected neighbors and cannot be promoted. If an even-indexed vertex cannot be promoted, its matching mate cannot be deleted; that retained occupied neighbor, together with the next even-indexed vertex’s selected support, prevents promotion of that next vertex. Induction from the left freezes the even indices, and induction from the right freezes the odd indices. This reasoning permits arbitrary orientations of a proposed bundle and survives the inclusion of other components.3. Both comb alignments have exactly zero receiver chargeThe receiver counts in Main Note §3 are correct.Fix a horizontal component of length  $2r$ , starting in column  $b$ . Choose whichever adjacent row belongs to its aligned tile row.For a full tile containing two consecutive path vertices, the other row contains exactly one selected support and one blank. The alternation provides the selected site. Component completeness excludes an additional endpoint, and the support constraints exclude an additional selected vertex.At a partial end tile, the axial support is selected. The site perpendicular to that axial support must be blank because the axial support already has its endpoint as an occupied neighbor. This rules out an exterior label that might otherwise have spoiled the endpoint-tile count.The complete counts are therefore:Starting-column parityReceiver tilesSelected vertices in receiverEndpoints in receiverReceiver charge $b$  even $r$  $r$  $2r$  $r+r-2r=0$  $b$  odd $r+1$  $r+2$  $2r$  $r+2+r-2(r+1)=0$ In the odd case, the  $r-1$  middle tiles each contain two endpoints and one selected vertex. The two end tiles contain
$$(t,p,b)=(2,1,1),\qquad (1,1,2),$$
in one order or the other. The endpoint perpendicular supports lie on opposite sides because the path has even length. Changing which adjacent row is paired with the path swaps the roles of those end tiles and preserves the totals.The argument includes  $r=1$ , when there are no middle tiles.The saturated correction is essential and is handled correctly. The saturated end tile has raw excess  $+1/2$ , but original charge zero. Its half-unit is restored at the deficient tile containing its endpoint’s actual mate. That mate tile belongs to the same receiver. For longer paths it can be an interior receiver tile, exactly as the main note states.There is also no boundary truncation. A terminal comb requires its outward axial supports and both alternating perpendicular sides. An embedding that would place one of these required selected vertices outside the physical rectangle cannot be a terminal comb. The blank extension therefore supports the proof without supplying any fictitious selected vertices.Rotation gives the vertical case. No separation between the collars of differently oriented components is needed: the ledger counts disjoint physical receivers.4. Single-promotion normalization proves the full stated square-free theoremLet  $v\in P$  have at most two occupied neighbors, and let  $u$  be its actual matching mate. The move is
$$T'=T\cup\{v\},\qquad
M'=M\setminus\{uv\},\qquad
P'=P\setminus\{u,v\}.$$
Its occupied set satisfies
$$A'=A\setminus\{u\}.$$
Since  $u$  is a neighbor of  $v$ , the promoted vertex has at most one occupied neighbor afterward. Every currently selected vertex retains feasibility because its occupied neighborhood only shrinks. This includes vertices promoted in earlier moves.The objective is preserved:
$$|T'|+|M'|=|T|+|M|.$$
One matching edge is removed, so the process terminates after at most the initial number of matching edges. Since  $P'\subseteq P$ , it creates neither a  $P$ -square nor an endpoint adjacency.Starting with no  $P$ -square, the final configuration is therefore square-free and single-terminal. Every remaining endpoint component is a straight even comb, and every one of its receivers has charge zero. Hence
$$|T|+|M|-\frac{mn}{2}
=
-\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q)\le0$$
for the terminal representative. Objective preservation proves the same coefficient-one inequality for the initial pair.A significant point is that the proof recomputes the receiver partition and tile charges at the terminal configuration. It does not assume that individual tile charges, saturation status, or receiver boundaries are invariant during normalization. Those quantities can change without affecting the argument.The exact deficit formula follows:
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
=
\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q).$$
Every summand is nonnegative, so equality holds precisely when each no- $P$  tile is saturated. This reasoning applies separately to every possible terminal representative; uniqueness of the normalization is unnecessary.5. The pure-rectangle reduction handles arbitrary actual matchings and exteriorsThe supplied rectangle proof covers its stated complete-component hypothesis.Completeness ensures that every occupied exterior neighbor of the rectangle is selected. Such a selected vertex already has an occupied neighbor inside the rectangle, so all its other neighbors are blank. This gives the support-row inequalities and the exclusion of two lateral supports at the same end.If all doubly supported corners have one grid color, promoting the other color on every matching edge removes all endpoints. The promoted vertices are independent inside the rectangle, and each has at most one exterior selected neighbor.The remaining case is the one requiring the switch argument: two doubly supported corners at opposite ends with opposite colors.Actual matching blocks and zero-support guardsThe  $V/HH$  decomposition follows from the leftmost remaining column of the actual perfect matching. Its vertices are either matched vertically to one another, or both must be matched horizontally into the next column. Removing that block gives the induction. Thus no matching edge crosses a block cut.For consecutive blocks,
$$v_D(b_i+1)\quad\text{and}\quad v_C(b_i)$$
lie in the same row at consecutive columns. Their perpendicular support sites are adjacent, proving
$$R_i+L_{i+1}\le1.$$
Because the final  $R$  is zero, there is a first block with  $R_i=0$ . If it is not the first block, the preceding  $R$  is one, forcing  $L_i=0$ . This proves the existence of the switch block for every width.The interpretation of a zero guard is complete. When an existing guard is an end corner, the chosen color makes it the corner opposite the doubly supported corner. Its lateral site is therefore blank. Thus  $L_i=0$  or  $R_i=0$  means that the corresponding guard has no occupied exterior neighbor, including a possible lateral neighbor.Both switch-block constructions are feasibleFor a  $V$  block, the only promoted vertices that can see a retained central endpoint are the two outside guards. Each has one such neighbor and no occupied exterior neighbor. Every other promoted vertex has at most one exterior selected neighbor and no occupied neighbor in its promoted-color region.For an  $HH$  block, the row  $q$  of the retained edge is correctly identified: it has color  $D$  at column  $a$  and color  $C$  at column  $a+1$ . Both outside promoted guards lie in that row.In the other row  $p$ , adjacent perpendicular supports cannot both be selected, so one endpoint has a blank perpendicular support and can be promoted. That central promoted vertex has:one retained vertical  $P$ -neighbor;a deleted horizontal mate;a blank horizontal neighbor outside the block, when present, because the promoted outside guard is in row  $q$ ;no perpendicular occupied neighbor;no lateral selected neighbor when it lies at an end, because the row- $q$  corner there is the doubly supported one.It therefore has exactly one occupied neighbor. The outside guards and all other promoted vertices satisfy the same bounds as above.The resulting occupied set is the old occupied set minus the deleted mates. This proves feasibility for all original selected vertices in the arbitrary exterior as well.The count is correct: the difficult case deletes exactly  $w-1$  matching edges and retains one, while the easy case deletes all  $w$ . Both are nonempty for  $w\ge2$ .The stated width-three sharpness example is also consistent. Full removal would force both endpoints of the middle vertical matching edge to be deleted, whereas the displayed two-edge bundle is feasible.Reductions composeDistinct original endpoint components have disjoint matching edges. For any vertex promoted by one component’s feasible bundle, the occupied set after applying all component bundles is a subset of the occupied set after applying that bundle alone. Feasibility therefore persists under composition.Moreover, deleting endpoints cannot merge endpoint components. After reducing the pure rectangles, every remaining component outside the prescribed capped class is square-free. Subsequent singles preserve that property. This proves the pure-rectangle extension of the coefficient-one theorem in all orientations.6. The capped mixed extension preserves its exact dependencyHere the dependency is specifically the charge
$$\rho(R_K)=-1$$
for a prescribed complete capped component  $K$ , with its specified matching, six supports, and an allowed tile-preserving placement and symmetry.The normalization preserves these hypotheses.First, the cap’s stated frozen property implies that its endpoints are initially single-terminal: an endpoint of occupied degree at most two would admit a feasible single promotion.Before any hypothetical first operation on that cap, operations on other components cannot remove any occupied neighbor of a cap endpoint. Every occupied neighbor outside the complete cap is an original selected vertex, and original selected vertices are retained. Its internal endpoints and matching are unchanged. Thus its endpoints remain of occupied degree at least three, so no first single promotion on the cap can occur.There is a further useful ownership fact here:Initial global single-terminality is unnecessary for excluding other-component endpoints from a capped receiver tile.If a tile contained a cap endpoint and an endpoint of another component, its endpoint subset would have to be the disconnected opposite-corner pair. The other two corners would be blank, contradicting terminality of the cap endpoint itself.Consequently, from the outset every tile of  $R_K$  contains only capped endpoints, original selected vertices, and blanks. Operations on other components change none of those labels:capped endpoints and their matching remain fixed;original selected vertices remain selected;original blanks remain blank because the occupied set only shrinks.Thus the receiver itself, its saturation data, and its matching transfers remain unchanged. Any prescribed blank conditions also persist. This verifies preservation of the permitted capped ledger under the normalization used in the main note.At termination there are exactly the original  $L$  capped components, and every other component is a square-free straight comb. Global terminal ownership makes all their receivers disjoint. The final ledger is therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
|T|+|M|-\frac{mn}{2}
&=\sum_{\text{combs}}0
  +\sum_{\text{caps}}(-1)
  -\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q)\\
&=-L-\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q).
\end{aligned}$$
Objective preservation gives the claimed exact identity
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
=
L+\sum_{Q\in Z}(2-t_Q),$$
and hence the strict bound
$$|T|+|M|\le\frac{mn}{2}-L.$$
Each capped component contributes its one receiver charge once. The no- $P$  tiles are counted only in  $Z$ , and saturated transfers are internal to the corresponding complete receivers.The accepted conclusions are exactly the stated square-free theorem, its complete pure-rectangle extension, and the prescribed capped mixed-component extension. The argument does not establish nonpositive charge for arbitrary terminal endpoint components or a universal grid theorem.
